title: The Christmas truce (1914)
hook: soldiers climb out of the trenches to sing carols and share food with the enemy
carry: silent night in no man's land

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new martyrs of Russia, and the word martys: a witness, faithful in small hidden ways.

A cold, clear Christmas Eve in Flanders. Two lines of trenches, close enough to shout across. Between them, a strip of mud, wire and shell holes the soldiers call no man's land. Anyone who raises his head above the parapet risks a bullet. Then, on the German side, lights appear: small candles, and in places little Christmas trees set up along the trench. A voice starts singing, and others join. Stille Nacht. Silent night. On the British side, men listen. After a while, someone sings back.

Much of what's known comes from soldiers' letters home. In places along the line, men climbed out of their trenches, unarmed, and walked toward each other. They shook hands and swapped what they had: chocolate, cigarettes, sausage, buttons from their uniforms, addresses to write to after the war. Some letters mention a kick-about with a ball. Both sides used the quiet to bury their dead, and in places they held services together over the graves. Then the truce ended, and the shooting started again. It didn't happen everywhere. In some sections the shooting never stopped. Officers on both sides disapproved, and it was not repeated the same way. So why does it matter? Because of what the soldiers sang. The carols told a story both sides knew: the angels over the shepherds' fields, singing, in the King James Bible, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." Men who had been trying to kill each other found they shared a song, a prayer and a holiday. Jesus once said, "Love your enemies." For a night, in a muddy field, some men did. This week, people kept stepping across something: the color line at Azusa Street, Pandita Ramabai's home for widows, Sundar Singh's water in an Indian cup, Harris the walking prophet, Kimbangu's church from a prison, the martyrs faithful in the camps. And now enemies sharing chocolate between the trenches.

Choose someone you're on the other side of: a rival at work, a relative you argue with. Notice the trench you've both dug, then picture one small thing you could hand across: a compliment you actually mean, a cup of coffee, a question asked out of real curiosity. You don't have to end the war; if you pray, pray for them by name.
Stille Nacht. The German carol German soldiers sang on Christmas Eve 1914, which British troops recognized and answered with their own voices across no man's land.
Your line: silent night in no man's land. For one night, enemies shared a song. A week of crossings, done.

howItsDone: At Christmas, churches sing carols such as Silent Night, and some retell the Christmas truce in services that pray for peace between enemies.

chat.says: Did the Christmas truce really stop the whole war for Christmas?
options: No. In places men met, swapped gifts and buried their dead, but elsewhere the shooting went on.
Yes, the whole Western Front fell quiet, and generals on both sides had agreed to it.
No, it was only a rumor: no soldiers' letters ever mentioned anything like it.
chat.meaning: Soldiers' letters tell of handshakes, gifts and shared burials in places, but it didn't happen everywhere, and the shooting started again.
